title: Mutation Types: Codons, Reading Frame, Point, Repeat, Translocation and Repair Defects
summary: Learn how start and stop codons define the reading frame, why in-frame dystrophin deletions usually cause Becker and frameshifts cause Duchenne, and how sickle cell, fragile X, CML, Lynch syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum illustrate the main kinds of DNA error.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 68 Hits 1, 13, 14 and 15 and Trap 4. Checked against Vitale 2025, Kearse 2017, Inusa 2019, Ciaccio 2017, Aartsma-Rus 2016, Sampaio 2021, Gallon 2021 and Leung 2022 (all read as Europe PMC full text). Context added: Hit 1 says the start codon is “always AUG”; Vitale 2025 says an open reading frame “typically” starts at AUG and Kearse 2017 describes non-AUG initiation at near-cognate codons such as CUG, GUG and UUG at lower efficiency (rv-aug-usual-not-always). Hit 14 and Trap 4 pair Duchenne with frameshift deletion and Becker with in-frame deletion; Aartsma-Rus 2016 says close to 10% of mutations do not follow the reading-frame rule and that duplications and small mutations, including nonsense point mutations, also cause Duchenne (rv-dmd-frame-rule-exceptions). Hit 15 equates xeroderma pigmentosum with an NER defect; Leung 2022 says the XP variant form (about 30% of cases) has normal NER and defective DNA polymerase eta (rv-xp-variant-not-ner). Not taught: the genetic code’s degeneracy (not stated in the sources read) and the reviewer’s phrase “hyperactive c-abl protein”, which the lesson gives as the source’s “persistently active tyrosine kinase”.

objectives: Name the three stop codons and the usual start codon, and explain how a nonsense mutation truncates a protein.
Predict Duchenne versus Becker muscular dystrophy from whether a dystrophin deletion keeps the reading frame, and state the rule’s limits.
Match sickle cell disease, fragile X syndrome, CML, Lynch syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum to their mutation or repair mechanism.

scenes.title: Two brothers, one gene
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two boys in one family both carry a deletion in the dystrophin (DMD) gene. Boy A lost exons whose combined length is a multiple of three; Boy B lost a stretch that is not. Beside them on the molecular bench: a sickle cell confirmation, a CML sample tested for t(9;22), and a colon tumour sent for mismatch repair testing. Question token: “Same gene, same kind of error, so the same disease?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: two brothers both carry a deletion in the dystrophin gene.
One brother lost a stretch whose length divides evenly by three. The other lost a stretch that does not.
Same gene, same kind of error. Will they have the same disease?

props.label: Same gene, same error, same disease?

scenes.title: Reading in threes
scenes.altText: Schematic mRNA strip divided into three-letter codons, starting at AUG and ending at a stop codon. Cards: “Start: AUG (usual)”, “Stop: UAA · UAG · UGA”, “Nonsense mutation: sense codon becomes a premature stop → truncated protein; many such mRNAs are degraded by nonsense-mediated decay”, and a note that near-cognate start codons (CUG, GUG, UUG) can also start translation at lower efficiency.

cues.text: A gene’s message is read in three-letter codons. The open reading frame usually begins at the start codon A U G.
It ends at one of three stop codons: U A A, U A G or U G A. Stop codons call in release factors and the finished protein is let go.
A nonsense mutation turns an ordinary codon into a stop codon too early. Translation ends prematurely, and many of these messages are destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay.
One caution: A U G is the usual start, not the only one. Cells can also start at near-matches such as C U G, G U G or U U G, but much less efficiently.

scenes.title: Four ways DNA goes wrong
scenes.altText: Four mutation-type cards. Point substitution: sickle cell, a single base change GAG → GTG puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain (HbS). Repeat expansion: fragile X, CGG repeats in the 5′ untranslated region of FMR1 — normal 5–44, grey zone 45–54, premutation 55–200, full mutation > 200 with promoter hypermethylation and silencing. Frame: a deletion or duplication whose length is a multiple of three keeps the reading frame (in-frame); any other length shifts it (frameshift), often reaching a premature stop. Translocation: CML, balanced reciprocal t(9;22)(q34;q11) fuses ABL1 (chromosome 9) with BCR (chromosome 22); the BCR-ABL1 protein is a persistently active tyrosine kinase.

cues.text: Point substitution. In sickle cell disease a single base changes, G A G to G T G, so valine replaces glutamic acid at position six of the beta-globin chain. That is haemoglobin S.

Repeat expansion. In fragile X, C G G repeats in the F M R 1 gene grow. Above two hundred repeats, a full mutation, the promoter is hypermethylated and the gene is silenced. Fifty-five to two hundred is a premutation.
Frame. If a deletion or duplication removes or adds a multiple of three bases, the reading frame survives. Any other length shifts the frame, and the scrambled message often hits a stop codon early.
Translocation. In chronic myeloid leukaemia, chromosomes nine and twenty-two swap pieces. ABL1 joins BCR, and the fusion protein is a tyrosine kinase that is always switched on.

scenes.title: Frame decides severity; repair genes guard the code
scenes.altText: Left: dystrophin cards. Duchenne: out-of-frame deletion/duplication or a nonsense mutation → no functional dystrophin → severe. Becker: in-frame change → shorter, partly functional dystrophin → later onset, slower progression. Footnote: close to 10% of mutations break this reading-frame rule; deletions about 68%, duplications about 11%, small mutations about 20% of DMD patients. Right: repair cards. Lynch syndrome: germline pathogenic variant in a mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); tumours often show microsatellite instability. Xeroderma pigmentosum: autosomal recessive; most forms are nucleotide excision repair defects, so UV photoproducts are not removed; the XP variant form (about 30% of cases) has normal NER but defective DNA polymerase eta; about 10,000-fold lifetime risk of non-melanoma skin cancer. Hook answer: Boy A (in-frame) most likely Becker, Boy B (frameshift) most likely Duchenne.

cues.text: Back to dystrophin. Out-of-frame deletions or duplications, or a nonsense mutation, leave no working dystrophin. That is Duchenne, the severe form.
In-frame changes make a shorter dystrophin that still partly works. That is Becker, often with later onset and slower progression. But close to ten percent of mutations break this rule.
Repair genes guard the code. Lynch syndrome is a germline variant in a mismatch repair gene: M L H 1, M S H 2, M S H 6 or P M S 2. Tumours often show microsatellite instability.

Xeroderma pigmentosum is recessive and mostly a defect in nucleotide excision repair, so ultraviolet damage is not cut out; the variant form instead lacks polymerase eta. So Boy A most likely has Becker, and Boy B Duchenne.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Becker is the worse dystrophy” (✓ Duchenne is severe: the frame is lost; Becker keeps the frame and is milder); “The bigger deletion is always the worse one” (✓ whether the frame is kept matters more than size, and about 10% of cases break even that rule); “Lynch syndrome is an excision repair defect” (✓ Lynch = mismatch repair; xeroderma pigmentosum = mostly nucleotide excision repair).

cues.text: Trap one: Becker is the worse dystrophy. No: Duchenne is severe because the frame is lost. Becker keeps the frame and is milder.
Trap two: the bigger deletion is always worse. No: whether the reading frame survives matters more than size, and about one case in ten breaks even that rule.
Trap three: Lynch syndrome is an excision repair defect. No: Lynch is mismatch repair. Nucleotide excision repair defects cause most xeroderma pigmentosum.

scenes.title: THE FAT CAT
scenes.altText: Memory aid: the sentence “THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT” read in three-letter words. Delete a whole word (“THE CAT ATE THE RAT”) and it still reads: in-frame, Becker. Delete one letter (“THE ATC ATA TET HER AT”) and every word after it is gibberish: frameshift, Duchenne. Second hook: “Lynch loses Mismatch, Xeroderma can’t eXcise.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: read THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT in three-letter words. Drop a whole word and it still reads: in-frame, Becker. Drop one letter and everything after it is gibberish: frameshift, Duchenne. And: Lynch loses mismatch, xeroderma can’t excise.

Where it breaks: about one dystrophin mutation in ten breaks the frame rule; Duchenne can also come from a single nonsense point mutation; and the xeroderma pigmentosum variant form has normal excision repair.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Frame kept → Becker · frame lost or early stop → Duchenne”, “Sickle = one base · fragile X = CGG repeat · CML = t(9;22) · Lynch = mismatch repair · XP = excision repair”.

cues.text: Read genes in threes: a deletion that keeps the frame usually gives the milder Becker dystrophy while a frameshift or early stop codon gives Duchenne, and the other classic errors are one swapped base in sickle cell, a CGG repeat in fragile X, a 9;22 swap in chronic myeloid leukaemia and broken repair in Lynch syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum.

props.label: Frame kept → Becker · frame lost or early stop → Duchenne
Sickle 1 base · FXS CGG · CML t(9;22) · Lynch MMR · XP NER

explanation.what: Plain language: genes are read three letters at a time, from a start signal to a stop signal. Errors can swap one letter, repeat a short phrase too many times, delete letters, or move a whole chunk to another chromosome, and some people inherit broken spell-checkers (repair genes). Scientific terms: codon, open reading frame, start codon (AUG), stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), nonsense mutation, premature termination codon, nonsense-mediated decay, point substitution, trinucleotide repeat expansion, premutation, full mutation, in-frame versus frameshift deletion, reciprocal translocation, BCR-ABL1, mismatch repair (MMR), microsatellite instability (MSI), nucleotide excision repair (NER).
explanation.why: Because the code is read in triplets, losing a multiple of three bases removes amino acids but keeps the rest of the message readable, while any other length scrambles everything downstream and usually reaches a stop codon early. That is why in-frame dystrophin deletions usually give a shorter, partly working protein (Becker) and out-of-frame ones give none (Duchenne). Repair defects do not cause one specific mutation; they let errors accumulate.
explanation.measure: Stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA; start usually AUG (near-cognate CUG, GUG, UUG at lower efficiency). Sickle cell: GAG → GTG, glutamic acid → valine at position 6 of β-globin. FMR1 CGG repeats: normal 5–44, grey zone 45–54, premutation 55–200, full mutation > 200 (promoter hypermethylation; more than 99% of fragile X). CML: t(9;22)(q34;q11), ABL1 + BCR. DMD gene: deletions about 68%, duplications about 11%, small mutations about 20%; close to 10% break the reading-frame rule. Lynch: germline MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 (EPCAM 3′ deletions silence MSH2). XP: autosomal recessive; most forms are NER defects (XP variant, about 30%, has normal NER and defective DNA polymerase eta); about 10,000-fold lifetime risk of non-melanoma skin cancer.
explanation.differs: In-frame (Becker, milder) vs frameshift or nonsense (Duchenne, severe); point substitution (sickle cell) vs repeat expansion (fragile X) vs translocation (CML); mismatch repair (Lynch) vs nucleotide excision repair (most xeroderma pigmentosum); premutation (55–200) vs full mutation (> 200).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify a stop codon, predict Duchenne or Becker from a deletion length, match a disease to its mutation type, or match Lynch syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum to the right repair pathway.

mnemonic.text: THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT: drop a whole word and it still reads (in-frame, Becker); drop one letter and the rest is gibberish (frameshift, Duchenne). Lynch loses Mismatch, Xeroderma can’t eXcise.
mnemonic.explanation: Shows why deletions that are multiples of three keep the downstream message readable, and pairs each repair syndrome with its pathway.
mnemonic.limitation: About 10% of dystrophin mutations break the reading-frame rule; Duchenne can also come from a single nonsense point mutation; real protein function depends on which domains are lost, not only on whether the frame is kept; and the xeroderma pigmentosum variant form (about 30% of cases) has normal nucleotide excision repair and a defective DNA polymerase eta.

questions.stem: A boy has a deletion of several dystrophin exons whose combined length is 255 nucleotides (a multiple of three). Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Becker muscular dystrophy: a shorter but partly functional dystrophin
options.rationale: Correct. A deletion that is a multiple of three keeps the reading frame, which usually gives a shorter, partly functional protein and the milder Becker form (about 10% of mutations are exceptions).

options.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy: no functional dystrophin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Duchenne usually results from out-of-frame deletions or duplications or from nonsense mutations, not from in-frame deletions.

options.text: No effect, because the deletion is in-frame
options.rationale: Incorrect. In-frame deletions still remove amino acids; the protein is shorter and only partly functional.
Incorrect. Fragile X is caused by expansion of CGG repeats in FMR1, not by dystrophin deletions.

questions.stem: Which pairing of disorder and molecular mechanism is correct?

options.text: Sickle cell disease: a single base substitution (GAG → GTG) in β-globin
options.rationale: Correct. One base change puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain, giving haemoglobin S.

options.text: Fragile X syndrome: reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22
options.rationale: Incorrect. t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome of CML; fragile X is a CGG repeat expansion in FMR1.

options.text: Chronic myeloid leukaemia: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion
options.rationale: Incorrect. CML is characterized by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)(q34;q11), which creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.
Incorrect. Most forms of xeroderma pigmentosum are nucleotide excision repair defects (the variant form affects DNA polymerase eta); defective mismatch repair is Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A single base substitution changes a codon in the middle of a gene to UAG. What is this mutation and its usual effect?

options.text: A nonsense mutation that ends translation early, giving a truncated protein
options.rationale: Correct. UAG is one of the three stop codons (with UAA and UGA); a premature stop truncates the protein, and many such mRNAs are degraded by nonsense-mediated decay.

options.text: A new start codon that adds amino acids to the protein
options.rationale: Incorrect. UAG is a stop codon; the usual start codon is AUG.

options.text: An in-frame deletion that removes one amino acid
options.rationale: Incorrect. No bases were deleted; one base was substituted, creating a premature stop codon.

options.text: A repeat expansion that silences the promoter
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeat expansion, as in fragile X, is growth of a repeated sequence such as CGG, not a single substitution.

claims.text: Stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA; AUG is the usual start; non-AUG near-cognate initiation exists at lower efficiency.
Nonsense mutation creates a premature stop, truncating the protein; NMD degrades many such mRNAs.
Sickle cell: GAG → GTG, glutamic acid → valine at β-globin position 6.
Fragile X: FMR1 CGG repeat ranges; full mutation > 200 with hypermethylation and silencing.
Reading-frame rule for Duchenne vs Becker; about 10% exceptions; mutation-type frequencies.
CML: t(9;22)(q34;q11) BCR-ABL1 fusion; persistently active tyrosine kinase.
Lynch: germline MMR gene variant (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); MSI-high tumours.
XP: autosomal recessive; most forms NER defects with UV damage unrepaired; XP variant has normal NER and defective polymerase eta; about 10,000-fold non-melanoma skin cancer risk.
Reviewer: the genetic code is degenerate (multiple codons per amino acid). Not taught; not stated in the sources read.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 68 Hit 1 says the start codon is “always AUG”. Vitale 2025 says an open reading frame “typically” starts at AUG, and Kearse 2017 describes translation initiating at non-AUG near-cognate codons (CUG, GUG, UUG) at lower efficiency. AUG remains the answer for “the start codon” on exams (register flag rv-aug-usual-not-always).

Ch. 68 Hit 14 and Trap 4 pair Duchenne with frameshift deletion and Becker with in-frame deletion. Aartsma-Rus 2016 says close to 10% of mutations do not follow the reading-frame rule, and Duchenne also results from out-of-frame duplications and small mutations, including nonsense point mutations (register flag rv-dmd-frame-rule-exceptions).

Ch. 68 Hit 15 and its memory hook equate xeroderma pigmentosum with a nucleotide excision repair defect. Leung 2022 says XPA–XPG act in NER, but the XP variant (XPV, about 30% of cases worldwide) has normal NER and mutations in DNA polymerase eta, which performs translesion synthesis. NER defect remains the best single answer for classic XP (register flag rv-xp-variant-not-ner).
